alignment.note: Greek opens with paratactic Καί ('And'), the characteristic Markan narrative connective; the Vulgate renders the transition with postpositive autem ('but/however'), introducing a mild adversative nuance absent from the Greek. The Syriac fuses the conjunction into the verb ܘܢܦܩܘ via prefixed waw, leaving no separate particle.

Greek and Latin both use an aorist/present participle (ἐξελθόντες / Exeuntes, 'having gone out / going out') in a circumstantial sense, whereas Syriac ܘܢܦܩܘ is a finite perfect ('and they went out'), coordinating the action rather than subordinating it — a typical Semitic preference for parataxis over participial subordination.

Greek εὐθύς and Latin statim are single adverbs ('immediately'); Syriac expresses the same notion idiomatically with the construct phrase ܒܪ ܫܥܬܗ (literally 'son of its hour'), a Semitic temporal idiom meaning 'at once/that very moment'.

Greek τῶν Ἡρῳδιανῶν and Latin Herodianis name 'the Herodians' as a partisan group; the Syriac renders 'those of the house of Herod' (ܕܒܝܬ ܗܪܘܕܣ) and appends ܘܡܠܟܐ ('and the king/royal party'), an explanatory expansion clarifying the political identity of the faction not present in the Greek or Latin witnesses.

Greek συμβούλιον ἐδίδουν ('were giving counsel', imperfect) and Latin consilium faciebant ('were making a plan', imperfect) employ a periphrastic idiom for plotting; Syriac compresses this to the single verb ܢܣܒܘ (root n-s-b, lit. 'they took'), reflecting the Semitic idiom 'to take counsel' without an explicit object noun.
